changes._why: the inner join from ProductInventory dropped a product with no inventory row, a stock of 0 and the most urgent
request: The warehouse refills the shelves. Show the products whose stock, over every location, is less than half their safety stock level, a product with no inventory row counting as 0, the lowest stock first; `ProductID` breaks a tie.
changes.sql:
SELECT p.ProductID, p.Name, p.SafetyStockLevel, COALESCE(SUM(i.Quantity), 0) AS Quantity
FROM Production.Product p
         LEFT JOIN Production.ProductInventory i ON i.ProductID = p.ProductID
GROUP BY p.ProductID, p.Name, p.SafetyStockLevel
HAVING COALESCE(SUM(i.Quantity), 0) * 2 < p.SafetyStockLevel
ORDER BY Quantity, p.ProductID

changes._why: PIVOT grouped by LastName alone, so two sales persons of one name would merge (Claude); sales persons without orders were left out, the years and the tie order unstated (Codex)
request: The sales director compares the sales persons over the years. Show every sales person's order subtotals for the fiscal years ending in 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025, a column per year, `0` for a year without sales; Adventure Works' fiscal year starts on the 1st of July.
`SalesPersonID` goes through the pivot, so two sales persons of one last name stay apart; the rows are ordered by the 2025 sales, the most first, then by `SalesPersonID`.
changes.sql:
SELECT pvt.SalesPersonID,
       pvt.LastName,
       COALESCE(pvt.[2022], 0) AS [2022],
       COALESCE(pvt.[2023], 0) AS [2023],
       COALESCE(pvt.[2024], 0) AS [2024],
       COALESCE(pvt.[2025], 0) AS [2025]
FROM (SELECT sp.BusinessEntityID AS SalesPersonID, p.LastName, h.SubTotal, YEAR(DATEADD(MONTH, 6, h.OrderDate)) AS FiscalYear
      FROM Sales.SalesPerson sp
               JOIN Person.Person p ON p.BusinessEntityID = sp.BusinessEntityID
               LEFT JOIN Sales.SalesOrderHeader h ON h.SalesPersonID = sp.BusinessEntityID
          AND h.OrderDate >= '20210701'
          AND h.OrderDate < '20250701') AS s
         PIVOT (SUM(s.SubTotal) FOR s.FiscalYear IN ([2022], [2023], [2024], [2025])) AS pvt
ORDER BY COALESCE(pvt.[2025], 0) DESC, pvt.SalesPersonID

changes._why: a customer may be a person buying for a store, both columns set, so COUNT(PersonID) and COUNT(StoreID) overlapped
request: Sales counts its customers. Show how many customers there are, how many of them are persons buying for themselves, how many are stores, and how many are persons buying for a store; the three kinds add up to the total.
changes.sql:
SELECT COUNT(*)                                                                         AS Customers,
       SUM(CASE WHEN c.PersonID IS NOT NULL AND c.StoreID IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)     AS Persons,
       SUM(CASE WHEN c.PersonID IS NULL AND c.StoreID IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)     AS Stores,
       SUM(CASE WHEN c.PersonID IS NOT NULL AND c.StoreID IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS StoreContacts
FROM Sales.Customer c

changes._why: ReceivedQty may be 0, so the division could fail; Vendor.Name is not unique, so the key breaks the tie
request: Quality assurance looks for unreliable vendors. Show the five vendors whose received goods were rejected the most, by the share of the quantity received, vendors with nothing received left out; `BusinessEntityID` breaks a tie.
changes.sql:
SELECT TOP (5) v.Name,
               SUM(d.ReceivedQty) AS ReceivedQty,
               SUM(d.RejectedQty) AS RejectedQty,
               CAST(SUM(d.RejectedQty) * 100.0 / NULLIF(SUM(d.ReceivedQty), 0) AS decimal(19, 2)) AS RejectedPercent
FROM Purchasing.PurchaseOrderDetail d
         JOIN Purchasing.PurchaseOrderHeader h ON h.PurchaseOrderID = d.PurchaseOrderID
         JOIN Purchasing.Vendor v ON v.BusinessEntityID = h.VendorID
GROUP BY v.BusinessEntityID, v.Name
HAVING SUM(d.ReceivedQty) > 0
ORDER BY SUM(d.RejectedQty) / NULLIF(SUM(d.ReceivedQty), 0) DESC, v.BusinessEntityID

changes._why: rejected (3) and pending (1) orders were counted as money spent; Claude's approved and complete orders, over Codex's 'all statuses, called order amounts'
request: The purchasing manager prepares the vendor reviews. Show the five vendors the company spent the most with, counting approved and complete purchase orders, `Status` 2 and 4, and how many such orders each one had; `BusinessEntityID` breaks a tie.
changes.sql:
SELECT TOP (5) v.AccountNumber, v.Name, COUNT(*) AS Orders, SUM(h.TotalDue) AS TotalDue
FROM Purchasing.PurchaseOrderHeader h
         JOIN Purchasing.Vendor v ON v.BusinessEntityID = h.VendorID
WHERE h.Status IN (2, 4)
GROUP BY v.BusinessEntityID, v.AccountNumber, v.Name
ORDER BY TotalDue DESC, v.BusinessEntityID

changes._why: a scrap reason means part of an order was scrapped, not that it stopped; TOP (5) on the sum alone had no tie-break
request: The plant manager looks for the costliest failures. Show the five scrap reasons with the most scrapped quantity, and how many work orders scrapped parts for each one; `ScrapReasonID` breaks a tie.
changes.sql:
SELECT TOP (5) r.Name, COUNT(*) AS WorkOrders, SUM(w.ScrappedQty) AS ScrappedQty
FROM Production.WorkOrder w
         JOIN Production.ScrapReason r ON r.ScrapReasonID = w.ScrapReasonID
GROUP BY r.ScrapReasonID, r.Name
ORDER BY ScrappedQty DESC, r.ScrapReasonID

changes._why: TOP (5) by a count alone was unstable at a tie
request: Marketing picks the countries for a mailing. Show the five countries with the most addresses; `CountryRegionCode` breaks a tie.
changes.sql:
SELECT TOP (5) c.CountryRegionCode, c.Name, COUNT(*) AS Addresses
FROM Person.Address a
         JOIN Person.StateProvince s ON s.StateProvinceID = a.StateProvinceID
         JOIN Person.CountryRegion c ON c.CountryRegionCode = s.CountryRegionCode
GROUP BY c.CountryRegionCode, c.Name
ORDER BY Addresses DESC, c.CountryRegionCode

changes._why: TOP (5) by revenue alone was unstable at a tie
changes.sql:
SELECT TOP (5) p.ProductNumber, p.Name, SUM(d.OrderQty) AS OrderQty, SUM(d.LineTotal) AS LineTotal
FROM Sales.SalesOrderDetail d
         JOIN Production.Product p ON p.ProductID = d.ProductID
GROUP BY p.ProductID, p.ProductNumber, p.Name
ORDER BY LineTotal DESC, p.ProductID

changes._why: TOP (5) by SalesYTD alone was unstable at a tie
changes.sql:
SELECT TOP (5) p.FirstName, p.LastName, t.Name AS Territory, sp.SalesYTD
FROM Sales.SalesPerson sp
         JOIN HumanResources.Employee e ON e.BusinessEntityID = sp.BusinessEntityID
         JOIN Person.Person p ON p.BusinessEntityID = e.BusinessEntityID
         LEFT JOIN Sales.SalesTerritory t ON t.TerritoryID = sp.TerritoryID
ORDER BY sp.SalesYTD DESC, sp.BusinessEntityID

changes._why: both recursive branches ignored StartDate and left out a row still effective with a future EndDate
request: Show every part of a product from its bill of materials effective now, down to the raw materials, with the quantity its immediate assembly takes and its depth; a row is effective from its `StartDate` through its `EndDate`, or with no end.
changes.sql:
DECLARE @productId int = 818;
DECLARE @asOf datetime = GETDATE();
WITH Parts (AssemblyID, ComponentID, PerAssemblyQty, BomLevel) AS (SELECT b.ProductAssemblyID, b.ComponentID, b.PerAssemblyQty, 1
                                                                   FROM Production.BillOfMaterials b
                                                                   WHERE b.ProductAssemblyID = @productId
                                                                     AND b.StartDate <= @asOf
                                                                     AND (b.EndDate IS NULL OR b.EndDate >= @asOf)
                                                                   UNION ALL
                                                                   SELECT b.ProductAssemblyID, b.ComponentID, b.PerAssemblyQty, p.BomLevel + 1
                                                                   FROM Production.BillOfMaterials b
                                                                            JOIN Parts p ON p.ComponentID = b.ProductAssemblyID
                                                                   WHERE b.StartDate <= @asOf
                                                                     AND (b.EndDate IS NULL OR b.EndDate >= @asOf))
SELECT p.AssemblyID, p.ComponentID, c.Name, p.PerAssemblyQty, p.BomLevel
FROM Parts p
         JOIN Production.Product c ON c.ProductID = p.ComponentID
ORDER BY p.BomLevel, p.AssemblyID, p.ComponentID

changes._why: Demographics is nullable and YearlyIncome optional in its schema, so a missing answer counted as a band of its own
request: Marketing segments the individual customers. Show how many of them answered each yearly income band of the survey stored in their Demographics document, the customers who did not answer left out.
changes.sql:
WITH XMLNAMESPACES (DEFAULT 'http://schemas.microsoft.com/sqlserver/2004/07/adventure-works/IndividualSurvey')
SELECT i.YearlyIncome, COUNT(*) AS Persons
FROM (SELECT p.Demographics.value('(/IndividualSurvey/YearlyIncome)[1]', 'nvarchar(30)') AS YearlyIncome
      FROM Person.Person p
      WHERE p.PersonType = 'IN'
        AND p.Demographics.exist('/IndividualSurvey/YearlyIncome') = 1) AS i
GROUP BY i.YearlyIncome
ORDER BY i.YearlyIncome

changes._why: the inner join left out a department with no current employee
changes.sql:
SELECT d.Name, d.GroupName, COUNT(h.BusinessEntityID) AS Employees
FROM HumanResources.Department d
         LEFT JOIN HumanResources.EmployeeDepartmentHistory h ON h.DepartmentID = d.DepartmentID AND h.EndDate IS NULL
GROUP BY d.DepartmentID, d.Name, d.GroupName
ORDER BY Employees DESC, d.Name

changes._why: Purchasing has no Advanced exercise; Claude's LAG over a yearly aggregate, on the approved and complete orders as AW_PURCHASING_I_01, over Codex's monthly running total of 2025
changes.title: The yearly spend with each vendor, against the year before
request: The purchasing manager watches how the spend with each vendor moves. Show, for each vendor and year, what was spent on its approved and complete purchase orders, the spend of the vendor's previous year with orders, and the change.
changes.sql:
WITH Yearly (VendorID, OrderYear, TotalDue) AS (SELECT h.VendorID, YEAR(h.OrderDate), SUM(h.TotalDue)
                                                FROM Purchasing.PurchaseOrderHeader h
                                                WHERE h.Status IN (2, 4)
                                                GROUP BY h.VendorID, YEAR(h.OrderDate))
SELECT v.Name,
       y.OrderYear,
       y.TotalDue,
       LAG(y.TotalDue) OVER (PARTITION BY y.VendorID ORDER BY y.OrderYear)              AS PreviousTotalDue,
       y.TotalDue - LAG(y.TotalDue) OVER (PARTITION BY y.VendorID ORDER BY y.OrderYear) AS Change
FROM Yearly y
         JOIN Purchasing.Vendor v ON v.BusinessEntityID = y.VendorID
ORDER BY v.Name, y.VendorID, y.OrderYear

changes._why: BusinessEntityAddress and AddressType, how every person, store and vendor reaches an address, are never read
changes.title: The addresses of each address type
request: The data steward checks how the addresses are used. Show how many addresses are held for each address type, the most first.
changes.sql:
SELECT t.Name, COUNT(*) AS Addresses
FROM Person.BusinessEntityAddress bea
         JOIN Person.AddressType t ON t.AddressTypeID = bea.AddressTypeID
GROUP BY t.AddressTypeID, t.Name
ORDER BY Addresses DESC, t.Name

changes._why: BusinessEntityContact and ContactType are read by no exercise
changes.title: An organization's contacts and their roles
request: The account manager wants the contact persons of a business entity and the role of each, ordered by last name, first name, person and role.
changes.sql:
DECLARE @businessEntityId int = 1492;
SELECT p.BusinessEntityID AS PersonID, p.FirstName, p.LastName, t.Name AS ContactType
FROM Person.BusinessEntityContact c
         JOIN Person.Person p ON p.BusinessEntityID = c.PersonID
         JOIN Person.ContactType t ON t.ContactTypeID = c.ContactTypeID
WHERE c.BusinessEntityID = @businessEntityId
ORDER BY p.LastName, p.FirstName, p.BusinessEntityID, t.ContactTypeID

changes._why: EmployeeDepartmentHistory is read only for its current rows; its history is what makes it interesting
changes.title: The employees who worked in more than one department
request: HR looks at internal mobility. Show the employees who have worked in more than one department, with how many departments each one worked in.
changes.sql:
SELECT p.FirstName, p.LastName, COUNT(DISTINCT h.DepartmentID) AS Departments
FROM HumanResources.EmployeeDepartmentHistory h
         JOIN Person.Person p ON p.BusinessEntityID = h.BusinessEntityID
GROUP BY h.BusinessEntityID, p.FirstName, p.LastName
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT h.DepartmentID) > 1
ORDER BY p.LastName, p.FirstName, h.BusinessEntityID

changes._why: Shift and its time columns are read by no exercise; time arithmetic across midnight
changes.title: Shift lengths across midnight
request: HR wants each shift's start, end and length in minutes; a shift that ends at or before its start ends the next day.
changes.sql:
SELECT s.ShiftID, s.Name, s.StartTime, s.EndTime,
       DATEDIFF(MINUTE, s.StartTime, s.EndTime) + CASE WHEN s.EndTime <= s.StartTime THEN 1440 ELSE 0 END AS DurationMinutes
FROM HumanResources.Shift s
ORDER BY s.ShiftID

changes._why: the nullable CurrencyRateID and CurrencyRate are read by no exercise; an outer join with COALESCE
changes.title: The orders and their amounts in each currency
request: Finance reports sales by currency. Show, for each currency the orders were paid in, how many orders there were, their total in US dollars, and their total in that currency; an order with no rate is in US dollars.
changes.sql:
SELECT COALESCE(r.ToCurrencyCode, N'USD')           AS CurrencyCode,
       COUNT(*)                                     AS Orders,
       SUM(h.TotalDue)                              AS TotalDueUsd,
       SUM(h.TotalDue * COALESCE(r.AverageRate, 1)) AS TotalDueInCurrency
FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader h
         LEFT JOIN Sales.CurrencyRate r ON r.CurrencyRateID = h.CurrencyRateID
GROUP BY COALESCE(r.ToCurrencyCode, N'USD')
ORDER BY Orders DESC, CurrencyCode

changes._why: the many-to-many SalesOrderHeaderSalesReason is never read
changes.title: The orders that gave each sales reason
request: Marketing asks why customers buy. Show, for each sales reason and its type, how many orders gave it, the most first, a reason no order gave included.
changes.sql:
SELECT r.ReasonType, r.Name, COUNT(hr.SalesOrderID) AS Orders
FROM Sales.SalesReason r
         LEFT JOIN Sales.SalesOrderHeaderSalesReason hr ON hr.SalesReasonID = r.SalesReasonID
GROUP BY r.SalesReasonID, r.ReasonType, r.Name
ORDER BY Orders DESC, r.Name

changes._why: the dated price history is never queried; a date-range lookup with a NULL end
changes.title: The list price of a product on a date
request: A customer disputes an old invoice. Show the list price a product had on a given date; a price runs from its `StartDate` through its `EndDate`, or with no end.
changes.sql:
DECLARE @productId int = 707;
DECLARE @onDate date = '2024-01-01';
SELECT h.ProductID, h.ListPrice, CAST(h.StartDate AS date) AS StartDate, CAST(h.EndDate AS date) AS EndDate
FROM Production.ProductListPriceHistory h
WHERE h.ProductID = @productId
  AND h.StartDate <= @onDate
  AND (h.EndDate IS NULL OR h.EndDate >= @onDate)

changes._why: WorkOrder is read only for scrap; its nullable EndDate against DueDate
changes.title: The ten products whose work orders finish late the most
request: The plant manager looks for late production. Show the ten products with the most work orders finished after their due date, and by how many days they were late on average; `ProductID` breaks a tie.
`AVG` of the integer `DATEDIFF` returns would truncate, so it averages a decimal.
changes.sql:
SELECT TOP (10) p.ProductID, p.Name, COUNT(*) AS LateWorkOrders, AVG(1.0 * DATEDIFF(DAY, w.DueDate, w.EndDate)) AS AverageDaysLate
FROM Production.WorkOrder w
         JOIN Production.Product p ON p.ProductID = w.ProductID
WHERE w.EndDate > w.DueDate
GROUP BY p.ProductID, p.Name
ORDER BY LateWorkOrders DESC, p.ProductID

changes._why: the coded Status, 1 to 4, documented only in the DDL's comment, is a CASE label and an enum mapping
changes.title: The purchase orders of each status
request: The purchasing manager checks the pipeline. Show, for each status of the purchase orders, how many orders there are and what they come to: 1 Pending, 2 Approved, 3 Rejected, 4 Complete.
changes.sql:
SELECT h.Status,
       CASE h.Status WHEN 1 THEN 'Pending' WHEN 2 THEN 'Approved' WHEN 3 THEN 'Rejected' WHEN 4 THEN 'Complete' END AS StatusName,
       COUNT(*)        AS Orders,
       SUM(h.TotalDue) AS TotalDue
FROM Purchasing.PurchaseOrderHeader h
GROUP BY h.Status
ORDER BY h.Status
